extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about a state beyond legal and illegal, attachment, birth and death, good and evil, characterized by eternal auspiciousness, fearlessness, indestructibility, immutability, purity, and freedom from disease.
Bhishma responds by recounting an ancient dialogue between Yajnavalkya and Janaka.

attributes.relationship: Bhishma transmits wisdom through historical example

extraction_text: Janaka asks Yajnavalkya about the number of senses, primordial substances, the unmanifest supreme Brahman, and what is higher than Brahman, along with questions about creation, destruction, and time calculation.
Yajnavalkya explains the principles of Yoga and Samkhya philosophy, detailing the eight primordial substances, sixteen modifications, and seven manifest entities.

attributes.content: Describes the metaphysical framework of creation

extraction_text: Yajnavalkya enumerates the eight primordial substances: the unmanifest (prakriti), the great (mahat), egoism (ahamkara), and the five elements (earth, wind, space, water, fire).

Yajnavalkya lists the sixteen modifications: the five sense organs (ear, body, eye, tongue, nose), the five sense objects (sound, touch, form, taste, smell), and the five action organs (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals), with mind as the sixteenth.

Yajnavalkya describes the ninefold process of creation: 1) emergence of the great/soul from the unmanifest, 2) emergence of egoism from the great, 3) emergence of mind from egoism, 4) emergence of five elements from mind, 5) emergence of five sense objects, 6) emergence of five sense organs, 7) emergence of five action organs, 8) emergence of upward and horizontal flows, 9) emergence of horizontal and downward flows.

attributes.conclusion: These constitute the nine creations and twenty-four principles according to scripture

extraction_text: Yajnavalkya explains the calculation of time for the unmanifest Brahman.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Cosmic time scale (ten thousand kalpas as a day and night of Brahman)

extraction_text: Brahman, upon waking, first creates herbs that sustain all beings.
Brahman creates Brahma from a golden egg.
Brahma sleeps in the egg for a year, emerges, becomes Prajapati, and creates the earth and heaven.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Divine sleep and creation of realms

extraction_text: Brahma arranges space between heaven and earth, as praised in the Vedas.
Brahma creates ahamkara (ego) and the subtle elements.
Brahma creates four sons before creating other bodies; they are ancestors of ancestors.
The senses are sons of the ancestors, and the world exists within the senses.
Supreme ahamkara creates the five great elements: earth, wind, space, water, and fire.
The five elements interact: they desire, help, identify with, and compete with each other.
The mind operates through the senses; senses do not perceive, the mind perceives.
The mind is the master of all senses, and all elements enter the mind.
Yajnavalkya transitions from explaining creation and time to describing destruction.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Cosmic cycles of creation and destruction

extraction_text: Brahma is beginningless, endless, and eternal, repeatedly creating and destroying beings.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Eternal divine activity of creation and destruction

extraction_text: The sun, urged by the Unmanifest, divided itself into twelve parts and burned all four types of beings (viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and sprout-born).
After burning the world, the sun flooded it with water, which was then consumed by the fire, leading to further destruction.
Wind consumed the fire and all heat, then space consumed the wind, mind consumed space, ego consumed mind, and the great soul consumed ego.
Prajapati Shambhu consumed the universe, described as subtle, all-pervading, and the supreme lord.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Ultimate cosmic absorption by a deity

extraction_text: The indestructible, unchanging, perfect creator of past, present, and future remains.
Yajnavalkya explains various philosophical views on the supreme soul, being, and deity, correlating body parts and senses with cosmic principles.
The speaker describes the three gunas (qualities) of primordial matter (Prakriti) and their manifestations.

characters: The Speaker (implied to be a sage or teacher)
The Listener (implied to be a king)
supernatural_elements: Description of cosmic principles (gunas) and their effects on beings

extraction_text: The speaker lists the characteristics of the sattva guna (goodness): joy, prosperity, purity, health, contentment, trust, humility, tolerance, non-violence, honesty, kindness, etc.
The speaker lists the characteristics of the rajas guna (passion): obsession with appearance, power, conflict, overindulgence, lack of compassion, agitation, hostility, greed, anger, pride, etc.

The speaker lists the characteristics of the tamas guna (ignorance): delusion, darkness, blindness, gluttony, excessive sleep, argumentativeness, indulgence in sensory pleasures, opposition to righteousness.
The text identifies this teaching as from Chapter 301 of the Shanti Parva (Book of Peace) in the Mahabharata.
Yajnavalkya (implied speaker) explains that the three gunas pervade all creation and that primordial matter transforms itself into countless forms.

supernatural_elements: Cosmological explanation of creation through gunas

extraction_text: Yajnavalkya states that those dominated by sattva ascend to heaven, those with mixed rajas and sattva become humans, those with rajas and tamas become animals, and those who transcend all gunas attain liberation.

supernatural_elements: Theory of rebirth based on gunas

extraction_text: Yajnavalkya describes the supreme state attained by wise ones as eternal, unchanging, fearless, flawless, and beyond birth/death.
King Janaka asks Yajnavalkya about the nature of the Supreme Being residing in primordial matter.
Yajnavalkya explains the distinction between the conscious Purusha (soul) and unconscious Prakriti (primordial matter).
Yajnavalkya describes Prakriti as inherently ignorant, operating through qualities (gunas), while Purusha is inherently conscious.

attributes: Purusha: conscious, aware of nothing higher

extraction_text: Yajnavalkya explains various epithets for the Supreme based on its creative functions (creator of entities, wombs, seeds, etc.).

divine_aspects: Creator of entities, wombs, primordial matter, seeds, qualities, destruction

extraction_text: Yajnavalkya uses analogies (reed vs. rush, mosquito vs. fig tree, fish vs. water, fire vs. pot, lotus vs. water) to illustrate the distinct yet coexisting nature of Purusha and Prakriti.

attributes.purpose: Clarify non-identity but connection between soul and matter
